title: The Beguines
hookLine: lay women living together to pray and serve in medieval cities, like Mechthild of Magdeburg

lines: A LITTLE TOWN BEHIND A GATE.
cards: Inside a medieval city, behind a wall and a gate, there's a little town of its own: small houses around a green, a chapel, a garden.
Women come back in the evening from nursing the sick, or sit at a loom, or teach children their letters. At night the gate closes, and the bell rings for prayer. These women are not nuns.
They haven't taken vows for life, and some could leave tomorrow and marry. But for now they've chosen to live here together, to pray, to work and to serve the city around them.

teach.b: The Beguines grew up in the cities of what is now Belgium, the Netherlands and Germany. They were lay women, ordinary Christians, who wanted the gospel life without entering a convent.
They lived in shared houses or walled courts called beguinages, earned their living with their hands, cared for the sick and the dying, and prayed together.
Their picture of life together goes back to the first Christians in Jerusalem, in Acts, in the King James Bible: "And all that believed were together, and had all things common."
The Greek word for in common there is koina. One Beguine became a writer.

teach.h: THE FLOWING LIGHT OF THE GODHEAD.
teach.b: Mechthild of Magdeburg lived as a Beguine in that German city and wrote a book called The Flowing Light of the Godhead, in German, the language of the street, not Latin.

It's full of love talk between the soul and God, bold and tender. In one passage she says, in effect, that a fish can't drown in water and a bird can't sink in the air, and the soul is made to live in God the same way.

Not everyone was comfortable with women living like this, outside the usual rules, praying and writing in their own words. Church leaders at times grew suspicious, and some Beguines were investigated or condemned.
Mechthild herself, late in life, went to live with nuns at a convent called Helfta. But the beguinages lasted, and you can still walk through some today. Women, together, in the middle of the city.

how: Some beguinages in Belgium and the Netherlands still stand and can be visited, and Christian lay communities today, women's and mixed, still live together to pray and serve their neighborhoods.

games.q: you're a young woman in a medieval city. you want a life of prayer and service, but not a convent. what do you do?
o: join the women living together in the beguinage.
games.why: Beguines lived together without lifelong vows, praying, working with their hands and serving the sick.

practice: Think of the people who live nearest you, on your street or in your building, not one at a time but together.

Let one small thing come that you could do alongside them, not just for them: a cleanup, a meal train, checking on an older neighbor. If you pray, hold your street in prayer; if not, hold the faces you know there.
